To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the existing evidence on the benefits and harms of screening does not justify participation rates as key performance indicator for preference sensitive screening programmes such as mammography.

participation rate as a key performance indicator for breast cancer screening programs is not reasonable, that informed choice rates are reasonable and that the practical challenges in measuring informed choice need to be addressed in further research.
participation rates should be replaced by informed choice rates in mammography screening programs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what the appropriate performance indicator should be for mammography screening, and why.
the ethical, methodological and practical challenges in the implementation of the principle of informed choice in mammography screening programs.
the question how to measure the performance of mammography screening programs in Europe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
participation rate is not an appropriate key performance indicator for screening, and informed choice rate is not yet a feasible alternative.
the European guideline for mammography screening needs to be amended by replacing the participation rate by an informed choice rate.
participation rates should not be used as key performance indicator for quality assurance in screening programmes, but that the informed choice rate should be considered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the European guideline for mammography screening needs to be revised.
informed choice rates should be used to assess quality of mammography screening programs, and that participation rates should be abandoned.
the European guideline for quality assurance should be changed to specify a minimum informed choice rate instead of a participation rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
informed choice rates should be considered as the key performance indicators for preference-sensitive conditions such as mammography breast cancer screening.
we need to move from the current performance indicator of participation to an informed choice rate.

we need to move from the "one-size-fits-all" approach to screening to an approach that is based on informed choices by the individual women and that we need to develop and test methods to measure informed choice rates.
